primary_cause: Semiconductor-sector de-risking tied to COVID demand and supply fears. Handset enterprise and industrial demand concerns
secondary_factors: General Crash Monday liquidation Apple and smartphone exposure and global growth fears. No major Broadcom-specific negative
store_description: Broadcom's 8.1% drop looks more like a sector trade than a company-event reaction. On March 9 investors were dumping cyclical tech as the oil shock and virus spread raised odds of a global recession which was especially painful for semis with handset and enterprise exposure.

primary_cause: No major Amazon-specific negative. Broad market crash and recession fears. Business actually seeing demand changes from COVID but stock traded as part of broad growth selloff
secondary_factors: Concern over logistics strain seller disruption labor and warehouse execution risk and advertising sensitivity. Later reframed as relative beneficiary
store_description: Amazon fell 5.3% even though the pandemic would later help e-commerce because on March 9 investors were indiscriminately reducing exposure to equities amid the oil collapse and worsening COVID shock. At that moment the market was still focusing more on global demand destruction and operational uncertainty.

primary_cause: No meaningful American Tower-specific negative. Forced selling in REITs and defensive yield names during cross-asset panic
secondary_factors: Liquidity-driven de-risking and concern that recession could slow leasing carrier spending or international operations
store_description: AMT's 5.9% decline looks primarily like a risk-off and liquidity event rather than a tower-business event. Even relatively defensive names sold off on March 9 as investors raised cash and repriced anything with equity financing or international exposure.

primary_cause: Repricing of companies exposed to small-business formation payroll and consumer tax activity amid COVID shutdown fears. Significant SMB exposure through QuickBooks
secondary_factors: General software multiple compression during the crash. SMBs already becoming clear COVID stress point
store_description: Intuit's 5.8% drop was likely driven by fears that virus disruptions would hit SMB customers payroll volumes and tax-related activity not by a discrete company event. On Crash Monday investors were rapidly discounting downstream damage to Main Street businesses well before relief programs existed.

primary_cause: No material Amgen-specific negative catalyst. Broad biotech and large-cap healthcare selloff as investors sold liquid winners and de-risked portfolios
secondary_factors: Concern that pandemic could disrupt physician visits drug administration clinical trials and biotech sentiment
store_description: Amgen's decline looks driven more by cross-market liquidation than by company news. Even high-quality defensive healthcare names were sold on March 9 as investors sought cash and cut risk across the board.

primary_cause: Semiconductor selloff tied to COVID demand and supply-chain uncertainty. High-beta multiple compression and liquidation of crowded growth names
secondary_factors: Growing fear COVID would damage electronics demand while disrupting Asian semiconductor supply chains. No fresh AMD-specific negative
store_description: AMD's 10.9% drop was steeper than the market because it sat in one of the most cyclically sensitive high-beta areas of tech. Investors were rapidly de-rating chip names on expectations of weaker PC gaming and broader electronics demand plus manufacturing and logistics disruption across Asia.

primary_cause: Chip-equipment sector selloff on expected slowdown in semiconductor capex and China and Asia disruption fears
secondary_factors: General tech liquidation and cyclicals underperforming in recession scare. No new Applied Materials-specific bad release
store_description: AMAT fell 9.9% because equipment makers are levered to customer capital spending and investors quickly assumed foundries and chipmakers could delay or trim orders if the global economy seized up. On March 9 that cyclicality mattered more than any company-specific development.

primary_cause: No Adobe-specific negative. High-multiple software selloff during liquidity shock
secondary_factors: Fears of slower enterprise spending SMB weakness and ad and creative customer pressure from COVID
store_description: Adobe's 9.2% decline looks mostly valuation-driven. Investors were slashing richly valued software names as recession fears rose and correlations went to one. Concerns about weaker enterprise budgets and pressure on smaller creative and marketing customers likely added to the move.

primary_cause: No major Abbott-specific negative. COVID test catalyst came later in March. Broad healthcare selloff and pre-test uncertainty
secondary_factors: Fear that elective procedure volumes and routine diagnostics could be disrupted by the pandemic
store_description: Abbott's 5.8% decline came before its later COVID-testing upside was recognized. At the time investors were still focused on broad healthcare disruption including weaker routine testing and procedure volumes as hospitals prepared for the outbreak.

primary_cause: No meaningful company-specific bad news. Actually received POSITIVE news Mar 3 — final European approval clearing path for Allergan deal. Broad market risk-off
secondary_factors: General pharma and biotech selling and merger-integration uncertainty amid worsening macro backdrop. Deal-related leverage concerns
store_description: Since the notable AbbVie-specific update in the window was positive the 4.0% decline appears mostly macro-driven. Investors were selling even defensive pharma names during the crash and deal-related leverage and integration risk may have modestly amplified the move.

primary_cause: Escalating COVID supply-chain and demand concerns worsened by Italy lockdown. Feb 28 Tim Cook said Apple closely watching COVID in South Korea and Italy where it had suppliers
secondary_factors: Broad tech selloff and smartphone demand fears. Explicit supplier and end-market exposure to regions most visibly worsening
store_description: Apple's 7.9% decline was more stock-specific than many other megacaps because it had explicit supplier and end-market exposure to the regions most visibly worsening. Cook had flagged South Korea and Italy on February 28 and when northern Italy locked down over the weekend that reinforced fears around both manufacturing continuity and European demand.

primary_cause: No company-specific negative. General market liquidation though consumer staples held up better than most sectors
secondary_factors: FX and emerging-market exposure plus broad recession concerns
store_description: Colgate's smaller 3.5% decline fits a defensive staples profile. It sold off but much less than cyclical tech banks and energy. No clear stock-specific trigger in the window so the move looks like broad de-risking with some concern about international exposure.

primary_cause: Growing concern over NBCUniversal theme parks film and advertising exposure to COVID. Later confirmed COVID would materially hit results
secondary_factors: Broad market crash offset only partly by defensive broadband business. Investors looking through stronger broadband to exposed assets
store_description: Comcast's 6.2% drop likely reflected early repricing of its non-cable assets especially theme parks film releases and advertising all of which were vulnerable to lockdowns and a recession. Investors were effectively looking through the stronger broadband segment and focusing on the parts most exposed to mobility and ad spending.

primary_cause: Anticipatory selloff on consulting and outsourcing demand risk from COVID. Later cut fiscal 2020 growth outlook to 3-6% from 6-8% on Mar 19 confirming fears
secondary_factors: Travel-dependent consulting model and broad tech and services multiple compression
store_description: Accenture's 8.2% fall suggests investors were already discounting delayed projects weaker discretionary enterprise spending and travel disruption before management formally revised guidance on March 19. The stock dropped first and the guidance cut validated that logic later.

primary_cause: Oil-price war and crude-price collapse. Saudi Arabia and Russia abandoned production pact both signaled higher output. Brent -23.9% WTI -25.1%. S&P energy index -20.1% largest one-day drop on record
secondary_factors: COVID demand destruction was already weakening oil market before the supply shock
store_description: COP's 24.8% plunge was overwhelmingly driven by the crude collapse not company news. With oil benchmark prices down roughly a quarter in a single session and investors suddenly repricing cash flow capex and balance-sheet risk across E&Ps ConocoPhillips was one of the most direct casualties of Crash Monday.

primary_cause: Consumer-credit and recession fears hitting card lenders and banks. Business mix especially sensitive to unemployment and consumer credit deterioration
secondary_factors: Falling yields expected credit losses and broader financial-sector liquidation. No Capital One-specific negative announcement
store_description: Capital One underperformed because its business mix is especially sensitive to unemployment and consumer credit deterioration. On March 9 investors were rapidly pricing in higher charge-offs weaker card spend and lower profitability from both recession risk and collapsing rates.

primary_cause: No IBM-specific negative event. Broad enterprise IT and consulting de-rating amid recession fears
secondary_factors: Concern customer spending decisions and services work would be delayed. Legacy and hybrid business mix offered less safe haven than cloud peers
store_description: IBM's 7.8% decline appears driven by the market assuming slower enterprise spending and project delays not by a discrete company catalyst. Compared with pure-cloud names IBM also had more exposure to legacy IT budgets and consulting activity that could be deferred in a shock.

primary_cause: Recession fears and discretionary retail selling. Before market recognized later stay-at-home home-improvement boom
secondary_factors: Concern that housing turnover contractor activity and large-ticket remodeling demand would weaken in a downturn. No major Home Depot-specific negative
store_description: Home Depot's 7.9% drop came before the market recognized the later stay-at-home home-improvement boom. On March 9 the dominant read-through was the opposite: lower consumer confidence weaker housing-related spend and a sudden stop in discretionary activity.

primary_cause: Violent financials selloff tied to recession fears and collapsing yields. Market-sensitive business mix made it more vulnerable than some traditional banks
secondary_factors: Exposure to capital markets trading-risk perceptions and fears dealmaking and asset values would weaken sharply. No Goldman-specific negative
store_description: Goldman's 10.4% drop was mainly a sector and macro move. Investors were crushing banks and broker-dealers as Treasury yields plunged and the probability of a severe recession jumped. Goldman's more market-sensitive business mix likely made it even more vulnerable during the panic.

primary_cause: Anticipatory selloff on digital advertising weakness and recession risk. Later reporting confirmed Google ad business slowed materially in March
secondary_factors: Broad megacap tech de-risking. Travel local business and brand advertisers cutting budgets
store_description: Alphabet's 6.2% decline looks tied to investors realizing that even dominant platforms were not immune if travel local business and brand advertisers cut budgets. The stock sold off before the slowdown was formally visible in earnings but later results confirmed March was the turning point for ad weakness.
